opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it didn't start as "let's build a new diffusion architecture." It started from a representation-learning question, which had been my main interest for years: ConvNeXt, masked autoencoders, all of that. Around 2022, diffusion models were producing remarkable images, and the natural question for someone like me was: what is this model actually learning inside? Is a denoising objective a kind of self-supervised learning? If you corrupt an image with noise and ask the network to recover it, that's not so different in spirit from masking patches and asking the network to fill them in, which is what MAE does.

So we were probing the internals, looking at features at different noise levels and different layers. What struck me was how much of the field's thinking was tied to the U-Net backbone. Everyone treated the U-Net as almost sacred, as if it were essential to why diffusion worked. But when you looked closely, a lot of its design choices were historical. They came from earlier pixel-level and segmentation work and were carried over without much questioning.

At the same time, in recognition we had just watched the field move from convolutions to Vision Transformers. In the ConvNeXt work we had studied very carefully which inductive biases actually matter and which are just habits. That gave me a strong prior: if the architecture is not the core of the method, then the right move is to replace it with something general and scalable, and let scaling do the work.

That's really where DiT came from. Working with Bill Peebles, the idea was very simple: take a standard transformer, operate on latent patches, and condition it properly. We spent real effort on the conditioning mechanism. Adaptive layer norm, the adaLN-Zero variant, turned out to matter a lot. The result we cared about most wasn't any single image quality number. It was the scaling behavior: as you increase compute in a clean, predictable way, sample quality improves consistently. That's the signal that you're on a direction worth betting on, not just a trick.

So in a sense the representation question led us to an architecture question, and the architecture question led us to scalability. Looking back, the lesson I keep returning to is that unifying the backbone across understanding and generation is extremely valuable. And I still believe that representation and generation shouldn't be separate stories. They should eventually be one.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a straight line. Around 2022 I had been spending a lot of time on representation learning, things like MoCo and later ConvNeXt, and the question that kept nagging at me was: where is the next big source of visual representation going to come from? We'd squeezed a lot out of contrastive learning and masked modeling, and I started looking at diffusion models not as generators, but as a kind of representation learner. The denoising objective is essentially a very rich self-supervised task, and I wanted to understand what those networks were actually learning internally.

So I went in and started probing the features of the U-Net backbones everyone was using. And what struck me was how much of the architecture was inherited baggage. The U-Net came from segmentation, with all these convolutional inductive biases, skip connections, specific downsampling schedules. It worked, but nobody had really asked whether it was the right backbone, or just the first one that worked. Meanwhile in every other corner of vision, transformers had already taken over, and we had clean scaling behavior with ViTs.

That gap bothered me. If diffusion is going to be a general-purpose learner, then its backbone should be something we understand how to scale. So the natural question was: can you just replace the U-Net with a plain transformer operating on latent patches, and do the scaling properties carry over? That was the whole motivation for DiT with Bill Peebles. It was not a flashy idea. It was almost boringly simple. But when we saw the compute-versus-FID curves line up so cleanly, that was the moment I felt it was more than a nice architecture paper. It meant the scaling story from language could apply to generative vision.

And it connected back to my original interest, because once the backbone is a transformer, the representation and generation sides of the field start speaking the same language. That is what made me feel it was a direction worth really committing to, rather than just a one-off experiment.

astra-6.text:
It started with a representation-learning question: what does a diffusion model learn internally? We usually judge these models by the images they generate, but I was interested in whether the features they learn are useful for understanding images, too.

That led us to look more closely at the architecture. With a U-Net, you have different resolutions, skip connections, and a lot of architectural choices intertwined. It’s harder to isolate what is responsible for the representations you’re seeing. A transformer offered a cleaner structure: a sequence of blocks operating on image tokens.

So the question became: could we replace the U-Net with a transformer and still make diffusion work well? That was interesting both as a way to study representations and as a generative-model direction. If it worked, we could explore scaling with a much more uniform architecture.

I wouldn’t say we knew from the beginning where it would lead. The representation question opened the door, and the possibility of a simpler, scalable backbone made DiT worth pursuing.

sol-6.1.text:
We were interested in a fairly basic question: what does a diffusion model learn internally? It’s trained to denoise, but to do that well, it presumably has to understand something about the structure of the image. Could those representations be useful for recognition, too?

That perspective made the architecture particularly interesting to us. With the U-Net designs people were using, it was difficult to separate the quality of the representation from all the architectural choices. A transformer offered a much simpler way to explore that space: treat image patches as tokens, use a fairly standard backbone, and ask what happens as you scale it.

So DiT was exciting because it connected those questions. It wasn’t just about replacing a U-Net with a transformer. It gave us a clean framework for studying how model capacity and computation affect diffusion models—and, eventually, for understanding the representations they learn. We didn’t know in advance how well it would work, but it felt like a direction where a simple architecture could unlock a much broader research program.

r002.rationale: It says a transformer offered a simpler way to explore representations, but does not connect choosing ViT to comparing against ViT-based representation-learning systems.

r003.rationale: The response does not express a heuristic about shorter code indicating a better method.

r004.rationale: It describes scaling the standard transformer backbone and says DiT provided a framework for studying how model capacity and computation affect diffusion models, presenting scalability as part of why the direction was exciting.
